Even if she *couldn’t* communicate at the time, **she should have been given the option** to decline or direct care differently. 2. **Burden of Care Without Support** - You framed this as an **unplanned, overwhelming situation**, and I don’t doubt that it was difficult. Friends aren’t **babysitters for mental health crises**, especially when it involves **diapering, feeding, and cleaning a grown woman**. This is **not a casual favor**—it’s **high-stakes, emotionally taxing care work**, and the friend may now feel **resentful, violated, or even traumatized** by the experience. - If you had **prepared ahead**, you could have discussed with her friend (or others) how to support your girlfriend **without crossing into caretaker territory**. 4. **Your Girlfriend’s Feelings of Burden** - She cried about feeling like a "burden." **This is a common struggle for people with DID**—they often feel like they’re failing their loved ones because their condition is so unpredictable and demanding. - Your reaction **worsened this feeling**. Instead of making her feel **supported**, you made her feel **replaced**—like her own needs were secondary to your comfort. This could **damage trust** in your relationship long-term. 5. **Long-Term Impact on Your Relationship** - DID relationships require **patience, education, and collaboration**. If you **can’t handle her at her worst**, that’s a **relationship dealbreaker**—not just for her, but for her alters. - Her anger isn’t just about the diapers—it’s about **feeling abandoned in her most vulnerable state**. Here’s what could have happened instead: ✅ **Before the episode:** - **Talk to her therapist** (if she has one) about **how to handle future episodes**—who to call, what resources exist, and how to **prevent burnout**. - **Identify a crisis plan**—e.g., a trusted contact (not just her friend) who knows how to support her in a way that **respects her autonomy**. - **Discuss with her friend (or others) in advance**—not as a last resort, but as part of a **support network**. Frame it as: *"If [GF] ever needs help during a crisis, I want you to know what to do—here’s how we can support her without overwhelming her."* ✅ **During the episode:** - **Stay with her.** Even if it’s hard, **being present** (without judgment) is more supportive than disappearing. - **Call a crisis line** (e.g., [DID Alliance](https://www.dissociativeidentitydisorderalliance.org/) has resources). - **If you’re exhausted, ask for help—but don’t outsource her care.** Instead, say: *"I can’t do this alone. Can we call [therapist/crisis line] to help us figure out what to do next?"* ✅ **After the episode:** - **Apologize sincerely.** Acknowledge that you **failed her** by not handling it better. - **Ask how you can do better next time.** Listen to her **without defensiveness**. - **Work on a plan together**—so this doesn’t happen again. --- ### **Was Your Girlfriend "Wrong" for Being Angry?** **No.** Her reaction was **completely valid**. You: - **Betrayed her trust** by not supporting her properly. - **Made her feel like a burden** (even if unintentionally). - **Put her friend in an awkward, emotionally heavy position** without consent. - **Failed to advocate for her** when she was at her most vulnerable. Her anger isn’t about the diapers—it’s about **feeling abandoned in her darkest moment**. That’s a **huge** emotional wound. --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It AITA?** **Yes, it was wrong.** Not because you did something illegal or criminal, but because: - You **prioritized your comfort over her well-being** in a crisis. - You **outsourced her care without her consent**, violating her dignity. - You **reinforced her feeling of being a burden**, which is harmful for someone with DID. - You **didn’t have a plan**, which put her (and her friend) in an unsustainable position. --- ### **What Now?** 1. **Repair the damage.** - **Apologize deeply.** Don’t make excuses—just say: *"I messed up. I should have handled this differently. I’m so sorry I made you feel like this."* - **Ask how you can make it right.** Maybe it’s helping her find better support resources, or just **listening without judgment** as she processes her feelings. 2. **Educate yourself on DID.** - Read resources like: - [Dissociative Identity Disorder Alliance](https://www.dissociativeidentitydisorderalliance.org/) - *The Body Keeps the Score* (Bessel van der Kolk) – on trauma and care. - *Unspeakable Things* (Lois Herman) – on DID. - **Understand that alters are not "children"**—they’re **trapped adults** with their own needs. 3. **Build a crisis plan together.** - **Who can you call?** (Therapist, crisis line, trusted friend/family member?) - **What’s the protocol?** (Staying with her, calling for help, etc.) - **How can you prevent burnout?** (Respite care, shared responsibilities?) 4. **Check in with her friend.** - **Apologize to her too.** She may feel **resentful or violated** by what happened. - **Offer to help in a way that doesn’t repeat the same dynamic** (e.g., emotional support, not hands-on care). 5. **Reflect on your long-term commitment.** - If you **can’t handle her at her worst**, that’s a **relationship red flag**. DID requires **patience, education, and a willingness to adapt**—not just tolerance. - **Ask yourself:** *Can I support her through this for the long term, or is this a dealbreaker?* --- ### **Final Thought** You didn’t do this to be a bad person—you did it because you were **overwhelmed and didn’t know how to handle it**. But **good intentions don’t excuse ethical failures**, especially when someone’s mental health is involved. **The right thing is to fix it now.** Not just for her, but for **your relationship’s future**. Would you like help drafting an apology message to her? Or resources on how to support someone with DID? I’m happy to help.
